en: Preface to the Re-engraved *Xuanqian Zhengshi* (Verification and Explanation of the Profound Commentary):

The minds of those who uphold the Way and the Dharma are like seals meeting their impressions; this complete reliance upon the *Wenju* (Textual Passages) is for the purpose of its circulation. Thus, Śākyamuni Tathāgata...

He appeared in the world for the sake of the one great cause and condition. He remained in the world for eighty years and preached the sutras in over a hundred thousand assemblies, taking the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as the foremost.
During the Chen and Sui dynasties, the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai personally realized the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Samādhi* and attained the *Pratyāhāra Dhāraṇī*.
He established the Eight Teachings, synthesized the Five Periods, and for ninety days expounded the Sublime [Dharma], composing commentaries on the *Lotus Sutra*.

The *Huakai xuanyi* (The Flowering of the Profound Meaning) was completed; through the perfection of the contemplation of the ten dharmas, emperors and elders were delighted and submitted, praising it.

The temporal teachings of a single era were fully and exhaustively elucidated. The Venerable Zhizhe Zhanran recorded the *Xuanyi* in ten fascicles, clarifying one thousand [points] of the mind-dharma and two thousand [points] of both Buddha-dharma and sentient-being-dharma.
He recorded the *Wenju* in fifteen fascicles, clarifying one thousand [points] of Buddha-dharma and [the remainder of] the mind-dharma.

The *Zhongsheng fa* (Dharmas of Sentient Beings) consists of two thousand [dharmas]. The *Ji zhiguan* (Record of Stopping and Contemplation), in twenty fascicles, clarifies one thousand dharmas of sentient beings;

together with the one thousand dharmas of the Buddha-dharma and the mind-dharma, they total two thousand. Thus, one comes to know the three thousand natures and characteristics (*xingxiang*) and the ten realms with their thousand suchnesses (*qianru*), which truly emerge from a single thought-moment of the person.
It is said: "When the mind arises, all phenomena arise; when the mind ceases, all phenomena cease. When one’s spiritual clarity is unclouded by delusion, sentient beings are themselves Buddhas.

When not yet awakened in a single thought-moment, the Buddha is himself a sentient being. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are equal and without distinction.
Master Zhizhe (Zhixuan) composed the *Xuanshan Shu* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning), a ten-fascicle work of proof and exposition, to open the way for people.
This is the true path of heaven; it establishes a bright lamp for the long night and reveals the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground for the sudden realization and entry of later students.
Alas, the original printing blocks of this book no longer exist, and extant copies are rare.

During the Xianfeng era, the Dharma Master Yanjing, the Lecturer at Mingyin Temple in Meixi, Tai County, conceived the aspiration to raise funds for its carving. Consequently, the Abbot of the temple undertook its construction.
In the lecture hall, there was no leisure; thus, he did not succeed in completing [the work]. He looked toward the assembly of monks and entrusted them, saying only:
"The one who shall complete this book must be you. (Mǐn Xī) also served as the abbot of Huázhǐng on Mount Tāi, Níngyì Guǎngrùn, and rebuilt Fólǒng Zhēnjué Tà Temple.
Time passed swiftly, and suddenly more than thirty years had elapsed. The Dharma sound remains.

How could I dare forget my heart’s intent? Thereupon, I continued to recruit fellow seekers from the various mountains—those of merit, wisdom, and good faith—to bring this work of virtue to completion.
May we all together enter the sublime assembly of the Dragon Flower; as the Wheel of Dharma turns, may we ascend together to Tuṣita Heaven.
This brief record of the causes and conditions for carving it upon woodblocks is offered solely with the hope that the many worthy ones will hold it dear. Thus it is said.
Written on an auspicious day in the autumn of the tenth year of the Guangxu era at Zhenjue Temple on Fulong Mountain by Minxi.

*Commentary on the Profound Meaning: Verification and Explanation*, Fascicle One. Composed by the Śramaṇa Zhishuan of Shaoshang. Regarding the "Preface to the Introduction to the Commentary on the Profound Meaning":

this refers to the preface that introduces the origins of the *Shiqian* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning); hence it is called the "Preface to the Introduction to the Commentary on the Profound Meaning."

The *Xiangjie* (Detailed Explanation) states: Regarding the term "Commentary on the Subtle Text" (*Shiqian*), when there were doubts concerning the *Xuanyan* (Subtle Text), the disciple produced the "pins" (*qian*) [i.e., the notes], and Jingxi explained them. Thus, the master and disciple are jointly designated.

It further states that the "pins" are the means of explanation (*nengshi*), while the *Xuanyan* is the object of explanation (*suoshi*). Regarding the term "one who removes hunger" (*chujin nan*): ancient translations rendered "śramaṇa" as "destitute.
Master Fayun stated that because he serves as a fertile field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), he is able to sever the destitution and hunger of sentient beings; therefore, he is so called.
He was a bhikṣu. The son of Pumen. According to the tenth fascicle of the *Fozu Tongji* (General Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), in the section on the collateral lineages of Jingxi:
Chan Master Pumen was of the He clan of Yueyang. His father, He Jie, served as the Magistrate of Yixing in Changzhou and settled there.

The Master was diligent in his studies from childhood and passed the jinshi examination, entering government service at court. One day, he realized the world’s vanity and unreality, and he withdrew his hairpin [to renounce office].
He shaved his hair and resided at Nanyue Temple. His only possessions were Confucian and Buddhist classics, along with hempen robes and sandals.
Later, he went to visit Jingxi to study the principles of *Zhiguan* and the *Lotus Sūtra*; he attained profound realization and was skilled in composition, cherishing ancient styles.
Jingxi respected him and treated him as a friend, for whom he composed the prefaces to the *Shiqian* and the *Fuxing*. He styled himself "Pu."

The Gatekeeper (the note states: Master Jingle of Jingshan Township in Yixing County was the preceptor under whom Jingxi studied; they were several *li* apart. There was also Yueshan Temple [in] Yixing—Yixing was changed to Yixing during the Song dynasty—and Guangxing Temple [in] Junshan, which according to the records belongs to Jiangyin County).

This preface is divided into two parts: first, the explanation of the origins of the *Zhiguī* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning); second, from "Universally" (*Pu*) onwards, the presentation of the intent for composing the preface.

Regarding the first, the origins, there are three sections: first, the appearance of the Tathāgata in the world and the existence of the wondrous sutra; second, from "The Text of the Sutra" (*Jīngwén*) onwards, Tiantai’s commentary on the sutra resulting in the *Xuánjì* (Profound Record);

third, from "Later Disciples" (*Hòjìn*) onwards, Jingxi’s propagation of the lectures resulting in the *Shìqiàn* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning). This further divides into two: first, the *Xuányì* (Profound Meaning) being without a commentary.

Difficult to understand. Next, regarding the section beginning with "Not far" (*bùyuǎn*), there are two parts: the *Shìqiān* (Explanatory Notes) and the clarification of its ease of understanding. First is the *Shìqiān*; second, from the section beginning with "Faith in what...

(*xìn suǒ*) onwards, is the praise for its ease of understanding. The first part [of the *Shìqiān*] also has two sections: first, the appearance in the world during a favorable time to propagate and lecture upon the *Xuányì* (Profound Meaning); second, from the section beginning with "Furthermore, according to the Dharma...
(*qiě fǎ*) onwards, the composition of the book through supplementation based on the propagation of the *Shìqiān*.

Regarding the phrase "the four teachings arranged in sequence," etc.: the "four teachings" refers to the four teachings of the transformative Dharma (*dharmaparyāya*). "Arranged in sequence" (*chenglie*) means that they include the sudden (*dun*) and so forth; it signifies their convergence. In the tenth fascicle of the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), Part 2, regarding the opening and closing based on the four dharmas, it says: "These are the four teachings. Based on the Perfect (*yuan*), one opens up the Distinct (*bie*); based on the Distinct, one opens up the Shared (*tong*); next, one opens up the Tripitaka (*sanzang*). Thus, through this sequence, they are brought together to merge with the Perfect. And so forth. As it is said: The four teachings are arranged in sequence. The first is the Tripitaka teaching; The second is the Shared teaching; The third is the Distinct teaching; The fourth is the Perfect teaching. The Tripitaka teaching is established for those who delight in the Lesser Vehicle. The Shared teaching is established for those who delight in both the Greater and Lesser Vehicles. The Distinct teaching is established for those who delight in the Greater Vehicle alone. The Perfect teaching is established for those who delight in the Great Vehicle. The Tripitaka teaching is established for those who delight in the Lesser Vehicle because it explains the Four Noble Truths. The Shared teaching is established for those who delight in both the Greater and Lesser Vehicles because it explains the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination. The Distinct teaching is established for those who delight in the Greater Vehicle alone because it explains the Six Perfections. The Perfect teaching is established for those who delight in the Great Vehicle because it explains the Threefold Truth. Furthermore, the Tripitaka teaching is established for those who delight in the Lesser Vehicle because it explains the Four Noble Truths as being characterized by suffering, origin, cessation, and the path. The Shared teaching is established for those who delight in both the Greater and Lesser Vehicles because it explains the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination as being characterized by ignorance, formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, existence, birth, and old age and death. The Distinct teaching is established for those who delight in the Greater Vehicle alone because it explains the Six Perfections as being characterized by giving, precept, patience, vigor, meditation, and wisdom. The Perfect teaching is established for those who delight in the Great Vehicle because it explains the Threefold Truth as being characterized by emptiness, provisional existence, and the Middle Way. Furthermore, the Tripitaka teaching is established for those who delight in the Lesser Vehicle because it explains the Four Noble Truths as being characterized by the three gates of liberation: emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. Coming now for this single period of teaching, I shall employ the Tripitaka, Shared, Distinct, and Complete teachings to establish the sudden and gradual approaches;
thus these four teachings are set forth in order. The purport of the *Lotus Sūtra*’s opening and unifying [the teachings] is contained within them.

Regarding the phrase "The ten sons having departed," the "ten sons" refers to the ten great disciples such as Śāriputra. These ten disciples were like the deaf and mute at the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Deeply...

He profoundly expounded the *Avataṃsaka*. In the *Āgamas*, he verified the attainment of the fruits; he elucidated the profound meaning of the Buddha’s concise teachings. He profoundly expounded the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*;

in the "Chapter on Disciples," the ten sons received their reprimands. He profoundly expounded the Vaipulya scriptures; this is identical to the *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra*, wherein Subhūti and others converted and taught the bodhisattvas.
He profoundly expounded the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the ten sons were each named and given predictions of enlightenment; he profoundly expounded the Dharma.

Flower. The commentary states that it is fully endowed with the merits of both the provisional and the real, yet its traces arise in five flavors to assist the Buddha in maturing sentient beings of the true practice.
Its profound assistance lies in human beings; since the "ten sons" have already passed away, it is said that [the teaching] is now severed.

Regarding the two lines beginning with "Only the three turnings," there are two meanings. First, concerning the contrast between the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) and the Perfect (Round) teachings: the three turnings of the Dharma wheel in the *Āgamas* pertain only to the Tripitaka.
Regarding the teaching: now the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* One Vehicle provides a second guidance; the opening of the *pitaka* is itself the Perfect [Vehicle]. As the Sūtra says:
"In the past, the Buddha first turned the wheel of Dharma at Vārāṇasī; now he again turns the unsurpassed, greatest wheel of Dharma. Second, regarding the sequential [teaching] of the single mind:
The *Āgama* represents the first turning; the *Vaipulya* (fangděng), the second turning; and the *Prajñā*, the third turning—these correspond respectively to the three truths (*trisatya*).

Now, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* guides beings toward the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), opening up these successive stages so that they become the single mind of the three truths (*ekacitta-trisatya*). (And so forth). **Mong Qiu (Seeking in Ignorance):** In the *Yījīng* (Book of Changes), the hexagram *Móng* states:
"The young and ignorant seek me. **Fù (Return):** In the *Fù* hexagram, the first nine-line (*chūjiǔ*) indicates: "Returning before one has gone far. Furthermore...
The Image says: "Returning before it is far. Regarding "the child being lifted up": Mencius said, "Even a child who has been lifted up knows how to love its parents.
Regarding "setting one's will on learning": Confucius said, "At fifteen, I set my will upon learning. "Receiving others with emptiness":
The *I Ching* states, "On the mountain is a marsh: this is Xian (Influence). The noble person, accordingly, receives others with emptiness. Bidan is the same as Bilin. Qin...
It was called Yanling; during the Jin dynasty it was called Bilin; during the Eastern Jin it was called Jinling; and during the Sui, Tang, and Song dynasties it was called Changzhou. Guoqing:
This refers to Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai, which was originally the site of the Crown Prince’s temple. Island Barbarians:

The *Kuodi zhi* states that the country of Wa (Japan) consists of more than a hundred small kingdoms situated on islands within the great southern sea. The phrase "How magnificent! is used to observe the bamboo slips.

**Joyful Speech.** "Never having encountered the sinews and ligaments (*kenkō*). The *Zhuangzi*, "On the Care of Life," says: "He cleaves the great cavities, guides through the great apertures, following their natural state.
He has never encountered the sinews and ligaments of the butcher’s knife, much less the large bones. **Shame at Not Reaching One's Goal.** The *Analects*, Upper Section, says:
"In antiquity, words were not uttered lightly; one was ashamed that one’s own practice did not reach [the words]. **Tiantai’s Naming of the Family.** [Tiantai] named his family [after this].

In antiquity, there were three meanings [to this]: first, it accords with the prophetic record of Dīpaṃkara; second, it turns one’s vows toward equality; and third, the practice of the Way has largely been centered at Tiantai.
Now, Jingxi did not forget his origins and was likewise called a Tiantai śramaṇa. Regarding "observing the images" (*guānxiàng*):

the commentary on the *Yijing* states that "images" refers to the two images (the upper and lower trigrams) of a hexagram, as well as the six lines within those two images. Regarding "striking the joints" (*jijie*): Zhaoran...
The end of the *Liu Shu* (Book of Liu) states: "There were many who struck their joints [in rhythm]. The commentary notes: "To strike the joints means to tap the essential beats.

The phrase "Am I alone not ashamed? borrows the language of Xiang Yu. "Tianwang" (Heavenly King) refers to Emperor Daizong of the Tang dynasty. "Yuebo" refers to Yue; "Shan" refers to the ancient state of Guo.

This refers to the outer walls of Shanzhou in Henan. The *Tongjian* states that on the day of Bingzi in the tenth month of the Gui-mao year during the reign of Emperor Daizong, because the regional governors (tu-fan) invaded Chang’an, Daizong took refuge in Shanzhou. The *Pumenzi* composed this preface in the following year, Jia-chen;
hence it says, "The next year after the Heavenly King was in the outer walls of Shanzhou" (*yue zai shanfu*), and so forth. The seventh month is called the month of the Prime Minister.
*Shiqian*, Scroll One, Part One. Regarding "Tiantai" and so forth: Tiantai is the name of a county. During the Eastern Han it belonged to Zhang’an;

during the Liang dynasty it was called Tiantai; during the Jin dynasty it was called Shifeng County. According to the seventh scroll of the *Fozu Tongji*: The Ninth Patriarch, the Venerable Jingxi Zhanran, was surnamed Qi.
His family had resided for generations in Jingxi, Jinling. Because people of the time revered his Way, [they named him accordingly].
This was his title. His family had traditionally practiced Confucianism; thus, he mastered learning at an early age. Even as a child, he possessed a transcendent ambition that surpassed the mundane.

At the age of seventeen, he went to seek the Way in the region south of the Xi River. There he met Fangyan of Jinhua, who transmitted to him the methods of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight).
In the eighteenth year of the Kaiyuan era, he first began studying under Zuoxi. When Zuoxi spoke with him, he recognized him as a vessel for the Way... (and so forth). Heaven...

During the Baoda calendar period, the court issued three successive edicts [summoning him], yet he declined each time on the grounds of illness and did not rise to the call. The Master first resided in Lanling.

He once traveled with forty renowned monks from the Yangtze and Huai regions to pay homage at Mount Wutai. There, Han Guang—a disciple of the Tripitaka Master Amoghavajra—addressed the Master, saying:
"Recently, while traveling through India with Amoghavajra, I encountered a Brahman monk who said he had heard that there was a Great Tang [in China]."

"The traces of Tiantai teaching can be used to discern the partial and the perfect, to distinguish the heterodox and the orthodox, and to clarify *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Is it possible that these could have been translated to this land?
Upon hearing this, the Master sighed and said: "It may be said that the Dharma was lost in the Middle Kingdom; seeking it in all four directions, it has finally returned to the Tiantai Peaks.
[The Master] wore coarse cloth and dwelt upon a single bed, instructing others through his own person without weariness even in old age. Great soldiers and... [text fragmentary].
During the period of famine, his disciples increased even further; they gazed upon the hall and chambers as their refuge.

On the fifth day of the second month in the third year of the Jianzhong era, he manifested illness at Fulong. Addressing his disciples, he said: "The Way has no fixed direction, and nature has no substance.
Whether one lives or dies, the underlying principle is consistently one. I shall leave my bones on this mountain; when my life-span ends tonight, I wish to speak with you all."

This is the definitive resolution of the Way. A single thought-moment devoid of marks is called Emptiness (*śūnyatā*); the fact that no phenomenon is not fully present is called Provisionality (*upāya*);

that which is neither identical nor different is called the Middle (*madhyama*). In the state of ordinary beings, these are the three causes; in the state of the Sages, they are the three virtues (*triguṇa*).

As one burns a wick, the beginning and the end share the same nature; as one traverses the ocean, the shallow and the deep flow differently. Self-benefit and benefiting others are exhausted within this alone—this is what you must resolve upon.
Having finished speaking, he leaned on his armrest and passed away. ○ *Xun* means "to tame" or "to be gentle. *Ma Shun* said, "To be *xun* is to attain the Way.
○ Ciyun said: "The *Xuanyu* and the *Jingxi* each have their own commentaries and exegeses, just as the Five Classics have the *Zhengyi* (Correct Meanings)."
○ A Personal Record of the Origins. The Fifth Patriarch, Venerable Zhāng'ān Guǎngdìng, was surnamed Wú and was a native of Zhāng'ān in Lín-hǎi.
When he was only three months old, he was able to follow his mother in reciting the names of the Triple Gem. Once, when a monk passed by their door, he said to the mother:

"This child is no ordinary person," [the master] said, and thus he was named accordingly. At the age of seven, he entered Shejing Temple to rely upon Hui-zheng, where he memorized ten thousand words daily.
At twenty, he received full ordination; endowed with innate wisdom and understanding, he never forgot what he heard once.

At the beginning of the Zhide era of the Chen dynasty, he visited Zhi-er at Xuanzhen Temple to receive instruction in the methods of contemplation (*guanfa*). After long and diligent study, he suddenly received his teacher’s seal of approval (*yinke*), and consequently...
As an attendant, he was able to fully comprehend and understand every Dharma-gate taught at whatever location he resided.

In the first year of the Zhengming era, he followed Zhiyi while he stayed at Guangzhai Temple in Jinling to listen to lectures on the *Lotus Sūtra*. In the summer of the thirteenth year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, he received the *Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra* (*Fahua xuanyi*) at Yushan in Jiangling.
In the summer of the fourteenth year, he received the *Perfect and Sudden Calming and Contemplation* (*Yuantun zhiguan*) at Yushan. Up to...

In the course of his lectures and expositions elsewhere, he compiled and transmitted more than one hundred fascicles of both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna scriptures, ensuring that what had not been heard before reached all;
all of this was due to the Master’s merit. ○ Regarding the Five Meanings of the Original and the Traced (Honji-Suijaku), the *Xiaqian* (Lower Commentary) states:

"Therefore, among the five chapters of the *Xuanyi*, none surpasses the Original and the Traced... (etc.). ○ Regarding the Eastern Diffusion: the final chapter of the "Yugong" ( Tribute of Yu) in the *Shangshu* (Book of Documents) says: "To the east..."
It gradually spread to the sea and reached as far west as the Flowing Sands. (The note says: *jiàn* [pronounced *jiān*] means "to soak" or "to permeate.

During the seventh year of the reign of Emperor Xiaoming of the Eastern Han dynasty, known as Mingdi, he dreamed of a sixteen-foot golden man with a halo of sunlight around his neck flying through the palace courtyard.
Fu Yi said, "I have heard that during the time of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty, there was a Buddha in the West. Thereupon, the Emperor dispatched the Court Gentleman...
He dispatched Cai Yin and others as envoys to the Western Regions to seek out the Buddha-dharma. After ten years, Cai Yin encountered Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna in Central India;
they obtained Buddhist images and Sanskrit scriptures and brought them back to Luoyang on white horses (and so forth).
○ [Regarding] Sui Wen Taiheng: Emperor Wen of the Sui Dynasty, whose personal name was Jian and whose family name was Yang, [was born at] Nanyue Si...

The Great Master [Huiwen] entered nirvana in the sixth month of the ninth year of the Dajian era of the Chen dynasty. The Dharma Master Zhi (Zhiyi) entered nirvana in the seventeenth year of the Kaihuang era of Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty.
Regarding the "three, five, seven, and nine vehicles": the three vehicles of the Tripitaka Teaching constitute the first three;

adding the human and celestial vehicles makes five; further adding the two vehicles of the Shared Teaching makes seven; and finally adding the Bodhisattvas of the Shared and Distinct Teachings makes nine.
[The titles] "Prince Wenxuan of Song" and so forth. (Upon examining the histories, there is only Prince Wenxuan of Jingling of the Qi dynasty, named Zi-liang, who was fond of Buddhism;

"When the provisional is fully perfected through contemplation, the principle is manifested by means of contemplation. ○ The "Appendix on Examples of Meaning Related to Phenomena" says: "As for the three contemplations, their meanings consist of only three types. First..."

First, following practice: one contemplates the single mind within the ten thousand objects. Although the ten thousand objects differ, their wondrous contemplation is equal in principle. Second, regarding the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*):
as in the texts on the Four Truths and Five Practices, one enters the single thought-moment to constitute the perfect contemplation. Third, relying on phenomenal appearances (*vastu-lakṣaṇa*):
as in naming Rājagṛha and Gṛdhrakūṭa based on their functions, one borrows phenomena as the object of contemplation to guide and transform clinging attachments. A detailed explanation [follows].

It is said: "The *Miaoxuan* (Profound Mystery) and the *Wenju* (Textual Commentary) each have their respective categories of 'dharmas' (*shifa*) and 'mysteries' (*xuan*). The *Xuan* (Mystery) refers to the four truths, the five practices, and so forth; this is the 'attachment to dharmas' (*fufa*).
Relying on matters such as response and resonance (*yinggan*) to cultivate contemplation is the 'reliance on matters' (*toshi*). (And so forth)."

The Five Chapters on Contemplating the Mind: "The mind is like a phantom or a flame. The detailed commentary states: "There are two parts to establishing practice: first, determining the object; second, applying contemplation.

What is meant by 'determining the object'? It is the establishment of the aggregates (*skandhas*). If one does not establish the aggregates, upon what basis would the sublime contemplation be applied?"

In what place do these wondrous objects manifest? Now, the mind being like an illusion or a mirage, its meaning is identical to that of the meditative object. Regarding the two metaphors of "illusion" and "mirage," they apply both generally and specifically.

In the *Zang* (Tripitaka) teachings, because phenomena have not yet been realized as empty, "illusion" is not mentioned. A detailed explanation states: generally, it refers to the illusion of being without substance due to dependent origination;
specifically, it is named the illusion of a single principle following conditions; and in the Perfect teaching, it is named the illusion where the nature subsumes cultivation.

Regarding the *māyopama-samādhi* (illusion-like samādhi), the fourth section on the noble practice of transcendent wisdom (*prajñā-ārya-caryā*) clarifies four types of wisdom regarding the Four Noble Truths.
The fourth is the wisdom of the unconditioned Four Noble Truths (*anabhisaṃskāra-catur-āryasatya-prajñā*). Based on the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, it extensively explains twenty-five royal samādhis:

from the *vimala-samādhi* which destroys the utility of the hells, up to the *ātma-samādhi* which destroys the utility of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). Within these...
Uttarakuru is destroyed by the *jvālāgnisamādhi* (Flame-Blaze Samādhi). Jambudvīpa is destroyed by the *māyopamasamādhi* (Illusion-like Samādhi).
In the southern continent, retributions are mixed; lifespans and other factors are indeterminate and like magical illusions. These arise from the mind as illusory karma;

from illusion arise views and afflictions (*kleśa*), from illusion arises ignorance (*ajñāna*), and from illusion arises nescience (*avidyā*). This continues until the illusions of views and afflictions are destroyed.

The conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is formed by illusion; when ignorance is destroyed, the illusion of the conventional truth is shattered. The ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is formed by illusion;

when ignorance is destroyed, the illusion of the middle way is shattered. Therefore, it is said that the Tathāgata is a great magician. In the twenty-fifth fascicle of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, the three samādhis appear within the fifth section on the sequence of practice.

Thus, their meaning extends to both the Perfect (*yuan*) and the Distinct (*bie*) teachings, whereas they have no place in the Tripitaka (*zang*) or Shared (*tong*) teachings. Regarding the contemplation of phenomena: it is the threefold contemplation within a single mind. Mind...
Contemplate its nature: it possesses nothing but names. As the Great Sūtra says, "To be able to contemplate the nature of the mind is called the supreme concentration.
Now, with single-minded wondrous contemplation, one contemplates the present momentary mind and sees only the three thousand wonderful provisional phenomena (*prajñapti*).

Since the provisional is itself emptiness, the mind is like a phantom or a mirage, possessing nothing but provisional names. Furthermore, since the mind arises from causes and conditions, it lacks self-nature (*svabhāva*), and so forth.
There are only names. Regarding the phrase "to say there is," this separately clarifies the three contemplations. First, the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*):

If one says the mind exists, one contemplates that the present momentary thought arises from the causes and conditions of *dharmatā*. Since these causes and conditions lack intrinsic nature, they are entirely empty in their very essence.

Thus, even a single momentary thought cannot be apprehended; how much less so the ten realms, the hundred realms, the thousand suchnesses, and so forth? This is the wondrous contemplation of emptiness.

If one says that the mind is non-existent, yet from the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*)—observing the three thousand realms of reality (*dharmatā*) up through the three thousand realms within the first stage of abiding (*prathamabhūmi*)—the response of the ten dharma-realms arises, then one can suddenly give rise to the images of the three thousand and ten realms; how much more so for a single realm or a single thought-moment?
This is the contemplation of wondrous provisionality (*miao-jiaguan*). Since it was stated above that existence is not existence and non-existence is not non-existence, then this mind...

The nature is neither existent nor non-existent; it cannot be conceived through existence or non-existence. Thus one knows that the mental characteristics of a single thought-moment in the present instant are neither arising nor ceasing, which is precisely the characteristic of quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirvāṇa*). Why is this? That it is not existent means it does not arise;

that it is not non-existent means it does not cease. This non-arising and non-ceasing is the characteristic of birthless quiescent extinction. Nāgārjuna said: "This is the characteristic of existence."
Quiescence is the quiescence of signlessness. Therefore, it is said that within a single thought-moment, the Middle Way is coolly manifest.
This is the wondrous contemplation of the Middle Way. The final phrase concludes that the mind is wondrous, for all minds are the one mind, and the one mind is all minds;
it is neither the one mind nor all minds, yet it is both the one mind and all minds—how could this not be wondrous? It is also...

In summary, this is the wondrous contemplation (*miaoguan*). The aforementioned contemplation of the mind is "wondrous. This "wondrous" refers to the contemplation of the mind as the "wondrous Dharma" (*miaofa*).

Since the aforementioned Middle Way wondrous mind is itself "wondrous provisional reality" (*miaojia*), it is said that "the wondrous is the three thousand [realms]. These three thousand realms of wondrous provisional reality are, by their very nature (*fadier*), within emptiness and the provisional;

they are thus the Dharma of the three wondrous truths (*miaosandi*). Therefore, it is said that "the three thousand are the Dharma," and the three truths are the three tracks (*sangui*). Thus, it is said:

Because it is the Dharma, it serves as the threefold model (*trimārga*). Since this model gives rise to wondrous understanding, it is called "the model. Below this, the contemplation of the mind (*cittabhāvanā*) constitutes the wondrous lotus that contains the essence (*tattva*), the doctrine (*siddhānta*), and the function (*vṛtti*).
The term "wondrous" (*miao*) serves as a general designation, yet it inherently contains the distinct meanings of essence, doctrine, and function.

Regarding the phrase "examining a single *kṣaṇa*," the contemplation of the mind is the wondrous sutra. The *Ratnaketuparivarta* (Renwang jing) states that ninety *kṣaṇas* constitute one thought-moment (*nimeṣa*); thus, a single *kṣaṇa*...

That scripture states that it takes nine hundred births and deaths [to exhaust the karmic traces]. This is the nature of mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*); material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) are likewise so.

Therefore, it says, "investigating a single *kṣaṇa*," and so forth. Furthermore, in Tiantai’s *Complete and Sudden Calming and Contemplation* (*Zhi guan*), one contemplates only the present single *kṣaṇa* of thought-mind, regardless of how many consciousnesses there may be.

As the ancients said: "The person of the Perfect Teaching cultivates contemplation and suddenly exhausts the eight consciousnesses. Who would say that one is contemplating only the sixth consciousness? ○

The mind is named "neither arising nor ceasing. The mind is itself the true mark (dharmatā). This means that observing the mind is itself the dharma-nature (dharmatā), which is produced by causes and conditions.
Since causes and conditions lack intrinsic nature, [the mind] is emptiness, it is the provisional, and it is the middle. The *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* says: "This dharma is both arising and ceasing.
Because it is identical with arising, it does not cease; because it is identical with ceasing, it does not arise. Thus, one knows that non-arising is precisely [this].
Emptiness. Non-extinction is precisely the provisional. That which is neither born nor extinguished is the Middle Way, the mark of quiescent extinction.
Therefore, the mind is itself the true reality (*dharmatā*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The true reality of all phenomena extinguishes all modes of contemplation.

The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* (or *Upadeśa-sūtra*, here referred to as the *Yijiao jing*): This sutra is a compendium of the four Āgamas; it reveals the Small Vehicle as the Great Vehicle, and is therefore cited here as well. One must not interpret this based on superficial or limited understanding.

The *Śālistamba-sūtra* (遗教经) and the mind of vitarka and vicāra (觉观心) belong to the teachings of the Hīnayāna and other such vehicles; these should be interpreted according to the present sūtra as being revealed and explained from the perspective of the Perfect Teaching (圆).
Regarding "arising together" (同起) and "arising separately" (偏起): in the Hīnayāna, the ten universal mental factors (大地法) arise together;

in the Dharma-lakṣaṇa school (法相宗), the five pervasive mental factors (五遍行) arise together, while the five object-specific factors (五别境) arise separately. Furthermore, within the numerical categories of the Hīnayāna, there are both those that arise together and those that arise separately. The mind is the source of all dharmas.

The Root. The detailed commentary states: "The mind is the root of all phenomena and the source of all afflictions. This is because the mind is capable of possessing [all things] and because the mind is capable of creating [them].
"Mind is the totality" means that it is explained as the foundation for all chapters; therefore, it is called the "totality. Totality signifies integration.

The three links—ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*)—and the seven links—consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), sensation (*vedanā*), birth (*jāti*), and old age-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*)—[are all contained within this totality].
Death. Second, the two branches exist within existence (*bhava*). *Miaole* says: "The nature-merits (*xingde*) are simply the three paths existing in their original state;
therefore, delusion, karma, and suffering are themselves the three virtues. *Fuxing* says: "In terms of principle, they are 'identical' (*ji*); in terms of phenomena, they must be 'separated' (*li*).

The differences in rank among the six destinies and the high and low levels of the four sages arise because the causes—the delusions—of the six destinies are different, the karma created is likewise diverse, and the resulting suffering of the six destinies differs accordingly.

There are also gradations in birth. Regarding the cessation of the mind of the four types of noble ones (*ārya*), there are four subtle divisions. Generally speaking, those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) cease the mind of six realms;

Bodhisattvas and Buddhas cease the mind of nine realms, or eight realms. Regarding the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) and the three paths within a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*), the *Myōraku* (Wondrous Joy) commentary states:
"A single thought-moment does not merely refer to the duration of one moment; it must be pointed to as..."
The mental factors are termed "a single thought-moment. The *Jinbi* states that afflictions, karma, and suffering are themselves the three causal natures of the rational essence (*li-xing*).

Apart from these three paths, all sentient beings possess no other distinct dharmas; therefore, affliction is the seed of the revealing cause (*liao-yin*), and karma is the seed of the supporting cause (*yuan-yin*).
Suffering (*duḥkha*) is itself the seed of the true cause; this refers to the "seed" (*bīja*). It is also the "nature-seed" (*prakṛti-bīja*). From the entirety of nature, cultivation arises.

One contemplates it through the wondrous Threefold Contemplation (*trividha-vipaśyanā*): suffering transforms into the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), delusion (*kleśa*) transforms into Prajñā, and karma (*karman*) transforms into Liberation (*vimukti*).
The ten realms and the three paths exist within a single kṣaṇa. Speaking in terms of the human realm: such characteristics are karma; such nature is delusion; such...

The substance is itself suffering. It is merely arising and ceasing. A person of perfect capacity (yuanren) contemplates the form and mind of the ten realms and likewise perceives their arising and ceasing, because the dharmas of the ten realms all arise from causes and conditions.

Yet, by being able to contemplate this very arising and ceasing as non-arising and non-ceasing, they transform the realm of conceptual thought (sīyì jìng) into the realm of the inconceivable (fǎsīyì jìng).
This is not something that can be reached through the contemplation of the mind or its analytical discernment by those of the three preceding vehicles.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom), Volume 41, states: "First is seated meditation (*dhyāna*).

One constantly contemplates the various parts, such as the bones of the body, which are combined together; thus it is called 'body. One then takes that which is being contemplated as a metaphor. Second is the recitation of sūtras."
Using the branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits of trees and plants as metaphors. Regarding "faith-practice" (śraddhā-carita) and "Dharma-practice" (dharma-carita):

the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states that hearing [the Dharma] constitutes faith-practice, while contemplation constitutes Dharma-practice; the *Sijiaoyi* (Meanings of the Four Teachings) says that faith-practitioners are dull-witted and Dharma-practitioners are sharp-witted, and so forth.

Regarding the discussion of the four propositions (catuṣkoṭi): see the end of the fifth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. Regarding the *Zhi Guan* (Calming and Contemplation), see the first record and the fifth fascicle of the *Fuxing*.

*Śata-śāstra*. Composed by Bodhisattva Āryadeva; explained by the Bodhisattva Vasu; translated by Master Kumārajīva. Two fascicles, upper and lower. In the "Refutation of the Self" (*Ātma-parīkṣā*) within the upper fascicle:
The non-Buddhist says, "The self has no tactile sensation and cannot be severed; it possesses only affliction. The Buddhist says, "If that were so, there would be no movement.
If the self has no tactile sensation, the body should not be able to reach other places. The non-Buddhist says, "It is like a blind person or a lame person. For example...

The blind and the lame rely on one another to be able to go. In this way, the spirit possesses the capacity for thought and the body possesses the power of motion; through their conjunction, they proceed. The internal [opponent] says:

Because their characteristics are distinct—just as the blind and the lame possess two different types of tactile sensation and two different types of volition—the dharma [of the body] ought to be able to go.

However, the spirit lacks these two functions; therefore, it should not be able to go (and so forth). Next, he cites Mouzi. Compiled by Sengyou of the Liang Dynasty in the *Hongming ji* (Collection for the Propagation and Clarification of Buddhism).
Fourteen fascicles. The *Mouzi Lihuo Lun* (Treatise on Mouzi Resolving Doubts) consists of thirty-seven chapters and is contained within the first fascicle.
○ Regarding the first record of *Zhi guan*, there is a single character error; it is found in the fifth record. The nineteenth fascicle of the Fangce edition states:

"During the reign of Emperor Xian of the Han dynasty, there was a man named Mouzi who deeply believed in the Buddhist school. He criticized and rejected the teachings of Zhuangzi and Laozi, composing a treatise in three fascicles consisting of thirty-seven chapters."
In the twenty-first section, "Rescuing the Śramaṇas by Discussing Right and Wrong," a question is posed: Laozi said, "The one who knows does not speak;
the one who speaks does not know. He further stated, "Great eloquence is like being dull-witted," and "The gentleman is ashamed when his words exceed his actions.

If a śramaṇa has attained the ultimate Way, why does he not sit and practice it, instead engaging in empty talk about right and wrong and vain arguments concerning what is crooked or straight? How can this be?
"Is this not a thief of virtue? He replied: "The aged also have their say. If they did not speak, how could I recount it? To know and yet not speak is improper;
to not speak because one does not know is the mark of a fool. One who can speak but cannot act is merely a teacher of the state;
one who can act but cannot speak is a useful servant of the state; one who can both act and speak is a treasure of the state. (3)

Within this chapter, it is stated that those who can neither speak nor act [according to the Dharma] are verily thieves of the state (and so forth). ○ Regarding the diligent practice of the three contemplations (*sanguan*):

one contemplates that within a single present moment of thought (*kṣaṇa*), there are the three thousand realms (*trisahasra-lokadhātu*) as empty, provisional, and middle. As for the six stages of identity (*liují*):

the detailed commentary states that the meaning of the six identities is contained within the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, while the term originates from Zhiyi’s *Mohe zhiguan*. Therefore, regarding the arousal of the great mind (*mahācitta*) within *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, it is manifested by means of these six stages of identity.
This is so. In the *Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra*, the character for "Buddha" (*buddha*) is explained according to the principle of the "six stages of realization" (*liu ji*).

Jingxi stated: "The meaning of these six stages originated from our own school; it profoundly accords with the perfect teaching. He further stated: "When the essence is non-dual, it is called 'realization' (*ji*"). Siming added: "Only when the essence itself is entirely [the Buddha] can it be named 'realization'.

Regarding the stages from "principle-realization" (*li ji*) up to "ultimate realization" (*jiongjing ji*), the detailed explanation in the first volume states: "The dharma-gate of the three thousand [realms]."

The fundamental nature of principle (*li*) is inherently possessed and is immutable. Jingxi said: "The myriad dharmas are True Suchness (*tathatā*); because they do not change, they follow conditions while remaining unchanging;
thus, the entirety of phenomena constitutes principle. Because the principle is identical, there is 'suchness' (*ji*).

In terms of phenomena, one discusses delusion and awakening, etc.; suchness is the transformation that creates the three thousand [realms]. The entirety of principle constitutes phenomena, thereby distinguishing the differences between the six stages; this is the differentiation within phenomena."
Therefore, there are six [aspects]. The two types of the three thousand—phenomenal and noumenal—are fundamentally characterized by the principle of perfect interfusion and mutual identity.
The noumenal aspect is the delusion regarding this; the stage of names and words is the understanding of this; and so on, up to the ultimate stage, which is the manifestation of this.

Now, taking the noumenal as identical yet the phenomenal as distinct, we differentiate within the undifferentiated when correlating them with the two types of three thousand. Because the phenomenal aspects differ, there are six; these are the phenomena that are identical to noumenon, contrasted with the three thousand produced through phenomenal conditions.

Because their principle is identical, they are "identical" (ji). This refers to the principle inherent within phenomena (*shiji*). It is in contrast to this principle that the three thousand realms are constructed. Furthermore, the *Four Foundations of Mindfulness* states:

"To understand the textual meaning of the fifty-two stages such that it flows through without obstruction constitutes 'identity in name' (*mingzijí*). The six levels of identity are distinguished according to their respective stages, as clarified in the sixth fascicle of the *Fashu*.
The seventh is the difference in assemblies. ○ The first fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "There are four *siddhāntas*: first, the worldly *siddhānta*;
second, the individual-person *siddhānta*; third, the remedial *siddhānta*; and fourth, the ultimate-meaning *siddhānta*.

○ One must possess the perfect and wondrous four *siddhāntas*. When the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the meaning of *siddhānta* applies to all three [vehicles]."
Therefore, one must distinguish [the teachings] by means of the fourfold *siddhi* (universal efficacy) of the Perfect [Teaching]. ○ The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* belongs to the Prajñā section;
it consists of ninety chapters, and Nāgārjuna’s commentary upon it comprises one hundred fascicles. ○ How can you take this as a general rule for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*?

You claim that since the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* comments on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, [the latter] is "one-sidedly wondrous" (*eka-miāo*) in terms of its teaching but "coarse" (*cū*) in terms of its section; thus, in terms of its section, it is coarse and not wondrous. Yet, regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, both in terms of its teaching and its section...
All are wondrous; therefore it is said, "The coarse and the wondrous are distinct" (and so forth). Regarding the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* as a comprehensive exposition:

the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* does not explain a single sūtra alone; thus, it is a comprehensive exposition. The *Vyākhyā* states that within the "Dependent Origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*) section of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it first poses the question:
"For what causes and conditions did the Buddha [teach this]? (and so forth). It subsequently provides twenty-three successive responses. These four *siddhāntas* constitute the [first]...

Seventeenth, furthermore, the text states: "The four *siddhāntas* comprehensively encompass all twelve divisions of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*) and the eighty-four thousand treasuries of the Dharma (*dharmakośa*);
all are reality" (and so forth). Regarding "the skillful means for refuting dharmas" and so on: in Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras, there are these three kinds of skillful means.

For example, as in the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra* (Logic Treatise), true refutation (*tattva-dūṣaṇa*) serves as the skillful means for refuting dharmas, while true establishment (*tattva-sādhana*) serves as [the skillful means for establishing them].

The establishment of the Dharma is a skillful means (*upāya*). These two [refutation and establishment] serve as skillful means for benefiting sentient beings. In the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, there are both refutations and establishments;

that is to say, after the preceding chapters of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* have exhausted the refutation of grasping at views—such as in the "Examination of the Four Noble Truths" chapter—[the establishment follows].
The establishment of the Three Jewels, the Four Noble Truths, and the four fruits of the śramaṇa corresponds precisely to the three types of Four Noble Truths and so forth within the Mahāyāna.

In the fifth fascicle of the *Zhiguan*, the lower section of the fifth part states: Someone raises an objection: "The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* speaks of 'neither arising nor ceasing,' yet this has not yet reached the profound principle.
Why? Afflictions (*kleśa*) are phenomena that arise; the shifting and passing away of the three marks [of conditioned existence] are phenomena that cease. It is simply that these do not arise..."

Because they are extinguished, it is said that they are neither born nor extinguished; this merely enters into emptiness (*śūnyatā*) without perceiving the meaning of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*).
The masters of the *Sammitīya* school explain that "neither born nor extinguished" means not non-born and not non-extinguished, thereby manifesting the Middle Way.

Tiantai says that while this interpretation supports the Middle Way, it harms the text and loses the true meaning. Why? Because Nagarjuna’s intent encompasses both the Shared (*pāryāptika*) and Distinct (*pratyekabuddha*) teachings; therefore, he says:

Birth is non-extinction. "Non-birth" refers to the non-arising within the twenty-five states of existence; "non-extinction" refers to the non-extinction through the transition and cessation of the three marks.

Since it can destroy the twenty kinds of *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (view of a self-body) and bring about the stages from *srotāpanna* up to *aśaikṣa*, how could this not be inclusive? This explains the underlying intent.
This also incorporates the intent of the Tripiṭaka: that which arises and that which ceases both belong to arising; Nirvāṇa is merely emptiness and belongs solely to quiescent cessation.
To be neither this arising nor this cessation is to simultaneously negate both extremes—does this not contain a distinct meaning?

If arising and ceasing are dharmas produced by causes and conditions, they are simultaneously empty, provisionally existent, and the Middle Way. Because they are empty, there is no arising. Because they are...
Because it is provisional, it is not extinguished. That which is neither born nor extinguished is precisely the Middle Way; this is exactly the Perfect [Teaching].
Interpreting according to the text, it simultaneously encompasses both [the Shared and Distinct Teachings] while specifically revealing the Middle; the four meanings are thus clearly manifest.
The four *siddhāntas* have ten layers. Regarding their names, there are similarities and differences: two names are identical, while two names differ.
The *Bodhisattvabhūmiviniścayasamgrahaṇī* (菩薩地持經), composed by Maitreya and translated by Dharmakṣema, states in its sixth fascicle:

"When a bodhisattva cultivates these three *samādhis*, they establish them in this manner and know them as they truly are. If there are other practices, they all enter the gates of these three *samādhis*, namely those of the śrāvakas."
Regarding what is studied and practiced, there are four *udāna* dharmas taught by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas for the sake of purifying sentient beings.
What are these four? "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent" is an *udāna* dharma. "All conditioned phenomena are suffering" is an *udāna* dharma.
"All things are selfless" is an *udāna* dharma. "Nirvāṇa is tranquility" is an *udāna* dharma.
The Dharma of *dāna*. All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are fully endowed with this Dharma and further transmit it to sentient beings;
this is called *udāna*. The various Muni-sages of the past, who were silent and tranquil, transmitted it to one another in succession;
this is called the "surging forth of the excellence of *udāna*. This continues until they are fully endowed and emerge from the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*); this is called *udāna*. ○ Mahāyāna.

The Single Seal: This is the seal of the single true reality (*ekalakṣaṇamudrā*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that within the Mahāyāna, it is taught that all phenomena are neither arising nor ceasing, possessing a single characteristic, which is to say, they are without characteristics (*animitta*).
The Three Seals of the Hīnayāna: According to the twenty-second fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is asked:
"What are the seals of the Buddha-dharma? It is answered: "There are three kinds of seals of the Buddha-dharma. The first is: all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*)..."
First, every moment of arising and ceasing is impermanent. Second, all phenomena are without self. Third, there is the quiescence of nirvana.

The practitioner knows that the three realms are entirely conditioned phenomena of arising and ceasing; they existed previously but now do not, and exist now but will not exist later, arising and ceasing in every moment.
Because they arise in a continuous succession of similar moments, they can be known and seen, like a flowing stream or the flame of a lamp.
A long wind appears to be a single entity because it flows in a continuous succession; thus, people regard it as one.

Likewise, within the midst of impermanent phenomena, sentient beings are constantly deluded, asserting that the "goer" is permanent. This is called the seal of the impermanence of all conditioned things. All phenomena are without self.
Within all phenomena, there is no master, no agent, no knower, no seer, no one who gives birth, and no one who acts.
All dharmas belong to causes and conditions. Because they belong to causes and conditions, they lack independence. Because they lack independence, they are without self (*anātman*).

Since the characteristic of a self cannot be apprehended, this is called the seal of non-self. As for "nirvāṇa," there is no nirvāṇa; [there is only] the extinction of the three poisons and the three decays.
Because the fire is extinguished, it is called the Seal of Quiescence (*śānti-mudrā*). Question: Why, within the Seal of Quiescence, is there only a single teaching and not many?
Answer: In the first seal, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are taught; in the second seal, it is taught that all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*) are without self (*anātman*).

Within the third seal, the fruits of the two seals are explained; this is called the Seal of Quiescence (*śamatha-mudrā*). Since all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are impermanent, one destroys the external five desires and so forth that belong to "mine" (*mama*).
If one speaks of non-self (*anātman*), one destroys the internal dharma of a self (*ātman*); for when both "self" and "mine" are destroyed, [quiescence is attained].
This is called the nirvana of cessation. When a practitioner contemplates conditioned phenomena as impermanent, they give rise to world-weariness and suffering.

Having known this weariness toward suffering, they maintain attachment to the subject of contemplation, thinking, "I am the one who can perform this contemplation. For this reason, there is a second seal of the Dharma (*dharmamudrā*):

knowing that all things are without self (*anātman*) within the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, and the twelve links of dependent origination, both internally and externally.

It is the Middle Way. ○ Chapter Twenty-five states: Zhan’an’s Commentary says, "The text is divided into three parts: first, the proclamation of the Middle Way;

If the sequence consists of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), and so forth, why is it said that there is birth and old age and death? The explanation states:
The later text says that consciousness in the present life is called "birth" in the future, while the six sense bases and so forth in the present are called "old age and death" in the future.

That which lies between them is precisely birth and death. To speak figuratively of the "middle way" means that two causes flank a single fruit, with the single fruit situated in the middle; it is thus.

In the treatise, this is precisely the meaning of the "Middle" (madhyama) as the negation of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). Why is it that merely [stating] that causes and conditions, and cause and effect, are neither arising nor ceasing is called the Middle Way?
Now, let me provide an explanation for easy understanding: ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) are the path of afflictions (*kleśa-mārga*) as perceived in the present.
To point to this path of afflictions is itself *prajñā*. That which is between them is the path of suffering (*duḥkha-mārga*), which is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). This is the Dharma-body.
This is precisely the Middle Way. If it is the Middle Way, then there is neither birth-and-death nor extinction. Because there is no birth-and-death, it is called "the destruction of birth-and-death.
The third [point] concludes that this is the Buddha-nature; since it is the Middle Way, how could it not be the Buddha-nature? Regarding the *Ratnakaraṇḍa Sūtra*:

within the *Mahāvaipulya Ratnakaraṇḍa Sūtra*, there is no passage concerning the three contemplations of the twelve links of dependent origination. It is likely that this refers to the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā Sūtra*. This...

The Sūtra clearly elucidates the meaning of the three contemplations regarding each of the factors. In the eighth chapter of the first volume, titled "On Coming and Going," Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is the meaning of 'coming,' and what is the meaning of 'going'? The Buddha replied: "'Coming' means the sense of turning toward; 'going' means the sense of turning away."

If there is neither turning toward nor turning away, neither coming nor going, this is the sphere of the noble ones (*ārya-gocara*). "Coming" has the meaning of delusion; "going" has the meaning of non-delusion.
That which is neither delusion nor non-delusion is the sphere of the noble ones. "Coming" is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); "going" is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

That which is neither conditioned nor unconditioned is the sphere of the noble ones (and so forth). Furthermore, it is said that "coming" has the meaning of self (*ātman*), while "going" has the meaning of non-self (*anātman*).
Meaning. It is neither self nor non-self; it is without coming and without going. This is the sphere of the noble ones' practice.
Even to the extent that "coming" has meaning and "going" lacks meaning, that which is neither existent nor non-existent is the sphere of the noble ones' practice.

Furthermore, in the subsequent section on the Middle Way (the ninth chapter), Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying: "Because the Buddha has taught the Dharma of non-duality, all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas..."
All are free from doubt and confusion, fully knowing the Middle Way; even ordinary persons are able to give rise to faith. The Buddha said that ignorance is non-dual.
Because it is non-dual, it constitutes the wisdom of non-three. This refers to the Middle Way which truly contemplates all phenomena.
Practice is non-practice, non-dual. Because it is non-dual, it constitutes the wisdom of non-three. Mañjuśrī, this is what is meant by the Middle Way.
With the perfection of the requisites, one truly contemplates all phenomena: consciousness is not consciousness, and so on up to old age and death, which are not old age and death.
Non-duality is likewise thus. Mañjuśrī, if ignorance were existent, that would be one extreme; if ignorance were non-existent, that would be another extreme.
Between these two extremes, there is no form, it is invisible, it has no location, it is without marks, and it is without dependence.
It is without defining marks. Mañjuśrī, this is called the Middle Way. It is the same for everything from the consciousness that performs actions (*saṃskāra*) up to old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).

This Middle Way fully possesses the true contemplation of all phenomena (*dharma*). All phenomena are non-dual. What is the meaning of "non-dual"? It is *madhyama*. (*Mad* means "not"; *yama* means "middle.
Not clinging to the middle—this is the meaning of *madhyama*). Why is that? Because one does not grasp at the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*) or the view of existence (*bhava-dṛṣṭi*).
For this reason, it is called *madhama*. As stated below in the sixth [fascicle], recorded in the annotations (*zhìqiān*) of the sixth fascicle, lower section;
it is cited among the three dharmas within the judgment of the Tripiṭaka Teaching (*sānzàngjiào*), as explained in the twenty-sixth fascicle of the *Fǔxíng* (Sub-commentary).
Third, the opening of the coarse. The body of the fourth dhyāna contains the branches and forests like a basin;

the coarseness of the emptiness of persons is like rice, while the subtlety of the emptiness of phenomena is like flour. All dharmas are the Mahāyāna—this is the intent of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

This is clarified in the "Chapter on the Broad Vehicle" (*Guǎngchéng pǐn*). Furthermore, the commentary on the twenty-fifth fascicle of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "The third section clarifies the chapter on the twelve links of dependent origination for bodhisattvas;

Furthermore, the passage "all ordinary beings" below clarifies that ordinary persons do not see [it]. The passage "only a Buddha can see" below the "Ten Abodes" (daśabhūmi) indicates that Bodhisattvas see it only slightly, whereas the Tathāgata sees it fully.
Since the Ten Abodes already involve seeing only a small portion at the end, they must likewise involve seeing only a small portion at the beginning.

As for why these perspectives are now presented interchangeably, it is precisely because one who reaches the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*) makes a single transition and immediately becomes a Buddha; thus, they are close to the final destination.
Therefore, it is said that one can see its end, yet its beginning is profound and obscure; thus, it is said that it is not seen.
Those in the Ten Abodes possess the path of cultivation capable of partial severance, whereby they can partially see its end, but cannot partially see its beginning.

As for the Buddhas who see both the beginning and the end, they ultimately know there is neither beginning nor end, and they ultimately mirror its beginning and end. In this text, from the perspective of arising from delusion, this is—

Furthermore, because one is born within the lineage of the Sage, it is called "entrusting oneself to the sacred womb. If one enters the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*), it is called "emerging from the sacred womb.

The Objects of the Four Truths. The *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-ekayāna-mahā-upāya-vipula-sūtra* (The Lion’s Roar of Queen Śrīmālā on the One Vehicle, the Great Skillful Means, the Vaipulya Sūtra) asks:

He is able to know all suffering, abandon all its origin, realize all its cessation, and cultivate all paths.
Therefore, O World-Honored One, conditioned birth and death, unconditioned birth and death, and nirvāṇa are likewise: they possess both the state with remainder and the state without remainder.
To explain the meaning of the noble truth of non-action (*asaṃskṛta-āryasatya*) is to explain the meaning of the immeasurable four noble truths. Why is this?

Because one is able, by means of one's own power, to know all suffering that is felt, to abandon all accumulation of feeling, to realize the cessation of all feeling, and to cultivate the path leading to the cessation of all feeling.
Entering the noble truths in this manner, the Tathāgata has taught the four noble truths in such a way as the four noble truths of non-action.
Meaning: Only the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has perfected the task; it is not the case that Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas have perfected the task.

7. The Mahākauṣṭhila Sūtra. Śāriputra asked: "Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila, is there any matter by which a bhikṣu, having accomplished the vision, attains right view and, regarding the Dharma, attains non-destruction, entering into the true Dharma?"
He replied, “There is, Venerable Śāriputra. There is a bhikṣu who knows nutriment as it truly is;

he knows the origin of nutriment, the cessation of nutriment, and the path leading to the cessation of nutriment as they truly are. How does he know nutriment as it truly is? It is said that there are four nutriments (and so forth).
How does he know the origin of nutriment as it truly is? It is because of craving that nutriment comes to be; this is called knowing the origin of nutriment.”

How does one know the cessation of nutriment as it truly is? It is said: "With the cessation of craving, nutriment ceases" (and so forth). How does one know the path leading to the cessation of nutriment as it truly is? It is said:

"The Noble Eightfold Path" (and so forth), extending even to ignorance, formations, and the rest. Regarding the four nutriments—namely, edible food (*kabaḷīkāra-āhāra*), contact (*phassa*), volition (*manosañcetanā*), and consciousness (*viññāṇa*)—edible food is also called "lump" (*kavaḍa*).
The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states: "Thus, the twelve links of dependent origination are none other than the Four Noble Truths."

"Non-arising. The first fascicle of the *Sijiao yi* (Meanings of the Four Teachings) states: "Previously, the principle of arising and ceasing was taken as the truth;

This is called the Noble Truth of Cessation. It is equal toward all phenomena; one attains the Way through the dharma of non-duality. This is called the Noble Truth of the Path.

Knowing craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and so forth constitutes the second, the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*). As the Sūtra says: "Knowing that the causal conditions of craving can give rise to the five aggregates is called middling wisdom. This refers to a single person.

The arising of love is immeasurable and boundless; it is that which Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas cannot know. To be able to know all such loves as arise in all sentient beings is called supreme wisdom.
[To know] "cessation" and so forth refers to the three truths of cessation (*nirodha-satya*). To know "this is the path" and so forth refers to the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*).
The Four Truths of the Path. Master Zhān’ān’s Commentary states: "The five aggregates (*skandha*) of ordinary beings and sages differ in their respective seeds;

within each aggregate, there are further distinctions of immeasurable realms (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*). How could these be known by the auditory disciples (*śrāvaka*) or the pratyekabuddhas? These are the immeasurable truths of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*)."
From the hells up to the Buddhas, karmic activities differ; each and every category of karmic activity has immeasurable aspects, which are not known even by those of the Two Vehicles.

This is the immeasurable Truth of Accumulation (*samudaya-satya*). From the hells up to the Buddhas, one must consider by what body and through what teaching the Dharma should be expounded so that beings may practice and learn.
Each and every bodily form and dharma is distinguished by immeasurable Dharma-gates (and so forth). This is [the Truth of Accumulation].
The Truth of the Path is immeasurable. From the hells up to the attainment of liberation by a Buddha, the causes and conditions differ;
furthermore, each instance of liberation possesses immeasurable modes of liberation (and so forth). This constitutes the immeasurable Truth of Cessation.

Regarding "Non-action" (*amala*): The *Sijiaoyi* (Meaning of the Four Teachings) states: "It is called non-action because it clarifies that the four realities do not constitute four [separate things].

Therefore, because all Buddhas and Tathāgatas, and even all phenomena (*dharma*), are suchness (*tathatā*). Regarding the "One True Truth" (*eka-satyam*):

Furthermore, Bodhisattvas directly transcend the Four Truths to enter the One Truth, namely, that all phenomena are neither arising nor ceasing, and so forth. Great...
Regarding the *Saṃvṛti-satya* (Conventional Truth) and so forth, Mañjuśrī asked the Buddha: "Is there conventional truth within ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*)?
Is there ultimate truth within conventional truth? The Buddha replied: "Conventional truth is itself ultimate truth. Mañjuśrī said:

"If that is so, then there are not two truths. The Buddha said: "There is a skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*). In accordance with sentient beings, I speak of the existence of two truths. As it is said:

That which is known by those who have transcended the world is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). That which is known by people of the world is called the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Next, Mañjuśrī asked about the true truth (*bhūta-satya*). The Buddha replied: "The true truth is that which is free from inversion (*aviparyāsa*).

Only that which is free from inversion is called the true truth. The true truth is that which is without falsehood (*mṛṣā*); if there were falsehood, it would not be called the true truth. It is eternal..."

To hold that there is pleasure, a self, and purity is what is called the meaning of the conventional truth. As for their reality, the two dharmas of existence and non-existence are mutually identical.
The Commentary states: "In the ultimate sense, the Middle Way possesses only a single essence; it is through skillful means, acting as conditions, that two are taught."

The four teachings that examine the true principle and so forth are explained according to their respective divisions (*dang-fen*). This means that within each division, the four teachings expound the true and central reality;
furthermore, it refers to the four masters turning the Dharma wheels of the *Zang* (Āgama), *Tong* (Shared), *Bie* (Distinct), and *Yuan* (Perfect) teachings.

That these constitute "a single-sound teaching" (*yi-yin jiao*) is a meaning that transcends the divisions (*kua-jie*), meaning that while, from the perspective of their respective divisions, it appears as though there are four masters preaching four distinct sets of teachings, this is actually taught by transcending those divisions.

How could there be teachings spoken by four Buddhas? It is simply that the Perfect One (the Buddha) expounds with a single voice. Since the teaching is one and unique, the practice and principle may be known accordingly, as can be understood from what was stated previously;

this is clarified in the "Distinguishing the Common and the Specific" section of the first volume of the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), regarding how [the teachings] encompass both their own respective divisions and transcend across them.
[This concludes the section on] the Extensive Refutation of Ancient Masters. Now, the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra* and other scriptures state: "World-Honored One, there are two kinds of Tathāgatas."
The Tathāgata-garbha containing emptiness. World-Honored One, the empty Tathāgata-garbha (etc.), and the non-empty Tathāgata-garbha (etc.). Regarding these two types of wisdom of emptiness:
the great śrāvakas are able to believe in the Tathāgata’s wisdom of the emptiness of all arhats and pratyekabuddhas.

It functions within the realm of the four non-perversions; therefore, that cessation of all suffering—which was previously unseen and unattained by all Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas—is realized only by the Buddha, who destroys the entire storehouse of afflictions.
One cultivates the path that extinguishes all suffering. World-Honored One, among these Four Noble Truths, three are impermanent and one is permanent. Why is this?

Because the three truths enter into the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*). That which enters into the characteristics of the conditioned is impermanent; that which is impermanent is a false and deceptive phenomenon (*mṛṣā-dharma*).

That which is a false and deceptive phenomenon is not a truth, is not permanent, and is not a refuge. Therefore, the truth of suffering, the truth of the origin [of suffering], and the truth of the path...
The truths are not the ultimate truth; they are neither permanent nor a refuge. The single Truth of the Cessation of Suffering is free from conditioned characteristics.

That which is free from conditioned characteristics is permanent. That which is permanent is not a deceptive phenomenon. That which is not a deceptive phenomenon is the truth, the permanent, and the refuge.
Therefore, the Truth of Cessation is the ultimate truth; it is inconceivable. This Truth of Cessation transcends all [conditioned] multitudes.
It is the object of the mind-consciousness (*citta-vijñāna*), yet it is not within the sphere of wisdom of all Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas.

The Wondrous Vehicle. The third of the three wondrous aspects—the wondrousness of the vehicle—is the wondrousness of the threefold opening.
